raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2 months history of intermittent headache and a 6-day history of left hemiplegia. She had been diagnosed with AIHA 8 months earlier and required immunosuppressive treatment with corticosteroids to maintain a hemoglobin level >65 g/L, when the patient was presented with anemia, edema, rash, and fever as main clinical features. At that time, she also suffered from eosinophilia and hypoproteinemia. Lung CT scans indicated a pulmonary infection. Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging showed lymphadenitis and excluded lymphoma preliminarily.
Two months before admission, increasing edema, rash, and fever developed again. Blood tests revealed eosinophil count 13.79 x 109/L (total white cell count 24.11 x 109/L, lymphocyte count 4.12 x 109/L). Blood parasites identification was negative and no organisms were cultured from it. Hypersensitive C-reactive protein levels fluctuated. Serology was negative for both syphilis and HIV. His medications were prednisone (20 mg/day, then tapered), albumin infusion, imatinib, antibiotic, and antiallergic drugs. During the treatment period, the patient complained of a headache for the first time, which was accompanied with an intermittent fever. Moreover, she developed visual problems, such as diplopia and reduced acuity. Aside from a stiff neck, her physical examination was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cell count 347 x 106/L, white cell count 147 x 106/L, glucose 4.47 mmol/L, protein 1.96 g/L, CSF IgM <6.94 mg/L, IgG 126 mg/L; the cryptococcus neoformans was detected in the CSF. Funduscopic examination shows binocular papilledema. Brain MRI showed increased enhancement of leptomeninges, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR)/T2 hyperintense in sulcus. The patient was given amphotericin B (AMB 40 mg/day) and voriconazole (0.2 g/day) treatment. Her headache remitted after 6 days. Repeat lumbar puncture after 2 weeks showed cell count 82 x 106/L, white cell count 82 x 106/L, glucose 3.16 mmol/L, protein 0.54 g/L, and again, cryptococcus neoformans was detected. Repeated brain MRI scans revealed new abnormal signal in the white matter of the bilateral ventricles and the basal ganglia areas (Figures 1A, B, 3A,B). However, no further examination was performed due to improved symptoms. She returned to the local hospital to continue treatment.
After 7 weeks of antifungal treatment, on February 23rd, 2018, the patient was referred to our department complaining of an increasing headache and a 6-day history of left hemiplegia. Clinical manifestations include intermittent low-grade fever, pneumonitis, altered mental status, and worsening visual problems. CSF examinations revealed cell count 297 x 106/L, white cell count 197 x 106/L, glucose 3.84 mmol/L, protein 1.13 g/L, CSF IgM 12.5 mg/L, and IgG 726 mg/L. No organisms (include cryptococcus neoformans) were detected in the CSF. Blood and sputum cultures were negative for any organisms. Treatments were switched from AMB and voriconazole to AMB and flucytosine. Repeated brain MRIs revealed significant lesions: a large, confluent area of FLAIR hyperintensity in the bilateral basal ganglia, and the white matter of the bilateral cerebral hemispheres, vermis of cerebellar, as well as the cerebellar hemisphere (Figures 2A-C, 3C,D). There was no evidence of restricted diffusion; however, there were signs of edema in the right hemisphere in addition to a midline shift of 0.9 cm. Enhanced T1 showed contrast enhancement in the bilateral basal ganglia, cerebellar vermis, cerebellar hemispheres (Figures 2D-H), not to mention bilateral leptomeningeal enhancement of the cerebral hemispheres. MRI imaging, obtained 1 month earlier, was significantly different from this presentation, but yet the PCR for CSF JCV DNA was negative (<2,000 copies/ml). Two weeks later, the patient's condition became even worse; a fever emerged, and she complained of lethargy and showed signs of altered mental status; 0.5 g/day x 3 methylprednisolone and symptomatic treatment slightly improved her symptoms. Unfortunately, she showed progressive neurologic deterioration and died of respiratory failure.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old woman on corticosteroids for autoimmune hemolytic anemia presented with a 2-month history of intermittent headache and a 6-day history of left hemiplegia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Eight months prior, the patient was diagnosed with autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) with eosinophilia, hypoproteinemia, rash, edema, and fever, managed with oral corticosteroids. Two months before referral, during a flare of marked hypereosinophilia (13.79 x 10^9/L) treated with prednisone 20 mg/day and imatinib, she developed headache, intermittent fever, diplopia, and decreased visual acuity, and was diagnosed at a local hospital with Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis and treated for 7 weeks with amphotericin B (40 mg/day) and voriconazole (0.2 g/day). Six days prior to referral on February 23, 2018, she developed worsening headache, left hemiplegia, low-grade fever, altered mental status, and worsening vision.
subjective.past_medical_history: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (diagnosed 8 months prior), hypereosinophilia, hypoproteinemia, lymphadenitis (lymphoma excluded by PET), and Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis (diagnosed 7 weeks prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for worsening headache, left hemiplegia, intermittent fever, diplopia, reduced visual acuity, rash, edema, and altered mental status. Home/recent medications: prednisone (20 mg/day tapered), imatinib, albumin, amphotericin B (40 mg/day), and voriconazole (0.2 g/day).

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation showed neck stiffness, diplopia, reduced visual acuity, and bilateral papilledema on fundoscopy; upon referral at week 7, exhibited left hemiplegia, altered mental status, lethargy, fever, and worsening visual impairment.
objective.routine_investigations: Prior flare showed WBC 24.11 x 10^9/L, eosinophils 13.79 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 4.12 x 10^9/L, fluctuating hs-CRP, negative blood parasites, negative blood and sputum cultures, and negative syphilis and HIV serologies.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial LP (2 months prior) showed total cells 347 x 10^6/L, WBC 147 x 10^6/L, glucose 4.47 mmol/L, protein 1.96 g/L, IgG 126 mg/L, and positive Cryptococcus neoformans (persisting at week 2 LP: WBC 82 x 10^6/L, protein 0.54 g/L). Referral LP at week 7 showed total cells 297 x 10^6/L, WBC 197 x 10^6/L, glucose 3.84 mmol/L, protein 1.13 g/L, IgM 12.5 mg/L, markedly elevated CSF IgG 726 mg/L, negative CSF JCV DNA PCR (<2,000 copies/mL), and negative CSF microscopy/cultures for C. neoformans. Referral brain MRI demonstrated extensive confluent FLAIR hyperintensities and contrast enhancement in the bilateral basal ganglia, bilateral cerebral white matter, cerebellar vermis/hemispheres, and leptomeninges with right hemispheric edema and a 0.9 cm midline shift.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis complicated at week 7 by fatal central nervous system immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome / post-infectious inflammatory leukoencephalopathy, confirmed by initial positive CSF C. neoformans testing followed at week 7 by sterile CSF with marked intrathecal IgG elevation (726 mg/L) and extensive confluent enhancing basal ganglia, cerebral white matter, and cerebellar lesions with 0.9 cm midline shift (JCV PCR negative). Switching from amphotericin B plus voriconazole to amphotericin B plus flucytosine and administering pulsed IV methylprednisolone (0.5 g/day for 3 days) yielded only transient improvement, and the patient died of progressive neurological deterioration and respiratory failure.
